metadata.name: mv
metadata.displayName: mv - Move or rename files and directories
metadata.description: Move or rename files and directories

installation.note: mv is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: mv (move) moves or renames files and directories. When moving to a different directory, mv removes the original file. When moving within the same directory with a different name, mv renames the file. Unlike cp, mv doesn't create duplicates - it moves or renames.
when_to_use: Move files to a different directory

syntax.description: Move SOURCE file(s) or directory(ies) to DESTINATION. If source and destination are in the same directory, it renames the file.

misconceptions.title: mv copies files
misconceptions.misconception: mv creates a copy like cp does
misconceptions.reality: mv moves files (removes original), unlike cp which copies (keeps original). Use cp if you want to keep the original file.
misconceptions.tip: mv = move (removes original). cp = copy (keeps original). Choose based on whether you need the original to remain.

misconceptions.title: mv needs -r for directories
misconceptions.misconception: mv requires -r flag to move directories
misconceptions.reality: mv works on directories without any special flags. Unlike cp, mv handles directories automatically.
misconceptions.tip: mv works on directories by default - no special flags needed

misconceptions.title: mv only moves, doesn't rename
misconceptions.misconception: mv only moves files between directories, can't rename
misconceptions.reality: mv can both move and rename. If source and destination are in the same directory, it renames. If different directories, it moves (and optionally renames).
misconceptions.tip: mv oldname.txt newname.txt in the same directory = rename. mv file.txt dir/ = move.

common_pitfalls.description: mv overwrites existing files without warning by default
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -i for interactive mode (prompts before overwriting) or -n to never overwrite. Or check destination first with ls.

common_pitfalls.issue: Losing files by moving to wrong location
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -v (verbose) to see what's being moved. Double-check destination paths. Verify with ls after moving.
Format is always: mv SOURCE DESTINATION. Last argument is always destination. If moving multiple files, last must be a directory.

common_pitfalls.description: Expecting file to remain after mv
common_pitfalls.solution: Remember: mv removes the original. If you need the original, use cp instead, or cp first then rm.

common_pitfalls.description: Moving between different filesystems is slower (copy + delete)
common_pitfalls.solution: mv works across filesystems but is slower. It copies then deletes. For large files, consider rsync or cp then rm.

related_commands.relationship: Copies files; mv moves, cp copies
related_commands.description: Copy files (keeps original) instead of moving

related_commands.relationship: Removes files; often combined with cp to simulate mv
related_commands.description: Remove files (cp + rm = mv behavior, but use mv instead)

related_commands.relationship: Rename files; mv can also rename
related_commands.description: Rename files using patterns (mv is simpler for single file renames)

related_commands.relationship: Advanced move/sync; more efficient for large directories
related_commands.description: Synchronize files and directories (advanced alternative to mv for large moves)

best_practices: Use -i for interactive mode to prevent accidental overwrites
Use -v for verbose output to see what's being moved
Use -n to never overwrite existing files
Use -b to create backups before overwriting
Verify destination exists before moving: ls destination/
Use -u to only move if source is newer than destination
Double-check paths before moving important files
Use ls after mv to verify files were moved correctly
performance_tips: mv is fast on the same filesystem (just updates metadata)
mv across different filesystems is slower (copy + delete)
For large directories across filesystems, rsync may be more efficient
mv preserves hard links when moving within same filesystem
Moving many small files may be slower than moving one large file

additional_notes.move_vs_copy: mv moves (removes original). cp copies (keeps original).
additional_notes.rename_capability: mv can rename files when source and destination are in the same directory
additional_notes.directory_handling: mv works on directories automatically - no special flags needed (unlike cp)
additional_notes.overwrite_behavior: By default, mv overwrites without asking. Use -i for safety.
additional_notes.cross_filesystem: Moving between filesystems requires copy + delete (slower than same-filesystem move)
additional_notes.preservation: mv preserves hard links and permissions when moving within same filesystem
